L57: # Linearization: Locally Self-Stabilizing Sorting in Graphs
L58: 
L59: Authors: cite25†Melih Onus , cite26†Andrea Richa , and cite27†Christian Scheideler cite28†Authors Info & Affiliations L60:

L69: cite0†Tools L70: ## Abstract
L71: We consider the problem of designing a distributed algorithm that, given an arbitrary connected graph G of nodes with unique labels, converts G into a sorted list of nodes. This algorithm should be as simple as possible and, for scalability, should guarantee a polylogarithmic runtime as well as at most a polylogarithmic increase in the degree of each node during its execution.
L72: Furthermore, it should be self-stabilizing, that is, it should be able to eventually construct a sorted list from any state in which the graph is connected. It turns out that satisfying all of these demands at the same time is not easy.
L73: Our basic approach towards this goal is the so-called linearization technique: each node v repeatedly does the following with its neighbors:
L74: 
L75: •
L76: 
L77: for its left (i.e., smaller) neighbors u_{1}, …, u_{k} in the order of decreasing labels, v replaces {v, u_{1}}, …, {v, u_{k}} by {v, u_{1}}, {u_{1},u_{2}},…, {u_{k − 1},u_{k}}, and
L78: 
L79: •
L80: for its right (i.e., larger) neighbors w_{1}, …, w_{ℓ} in the order of increasing labels, v replaces {v, w_{1}}, …, {v, w_{ℓ}} by {v, w_{1}}, {w_{1}, w_{2}}, …, {w_{ℓ − 1}, w_{ℓ}}.
L81: As shown in this paper, this technique transforms any connected graph into a sorted list, but there are graphs for which this can take a long time. Hence, we propose several extensions of the linearization technique and experimentally evaluate their performance. Our results indicate that some of these have a polylogarithmic performance, so there is hope that there are distributed algorithms that can achieve all of our goals above.

L6: # Self-stabilizing ring networks on connected graphs
L7: 
L8: Cramer, Curt; Fuhrmann, Thomas
L9: ## Abstract:
L10: Large networks require scalable routing. Traditionally, protocol
L11: overhead is
L12: reduced by introducing a hierarchy. This requires aggregation of
L13: nearby nodes
L14: under a common address prefix. In fixed networks, this is achieved
L15: administratively, whereas in wireless ad-hoc networks, dynamic
L16: assignments of
L17: nodes to aggregation units are required.
L18: As a result of the nodes commonly being assigned a random
L19: network address, the
L20: majority of proposed ad-hoc routing protocols discovers routes
L21: between end
L22: nodes by flooding, thus limiting the network size. Peer-to-peer
L23: (P2P) overlay
L24: networks offer scalable routing solutions by employing
L25: virtualized address spaces,
L26: yet assume an underlying routing protocol for end-to-end
L27: connectivity.
L28: We investigate a cross-layer approach to P2P routing, where the
L29: virtual address
L30: space is implemented with a network-layer routing protocol by
L31: itself. The Iterative
L32: Successor Pointer Rewiring Protocol (ISPRP) efficiently
L33: initializes a ring-structured
L34: network among nodes having but link-layer connectivity. It is
L35: fully self-organizing
L36: and issues only a small per-node amount of messages by keeping
L37: interactions
L38: between nodes as local as possible.
L39: ... mehr
L40: The main contribution of this paper is a proof that ISPRP is
L41: self-stabilizing, that is,
L42: starting from an arbitrary initial state, the protocol lets the
L43: network converge into
L44: a correct state within a bounded amount of time.

L9: # Title:Towards Learning-Augmented Peer-to-Peer Networks: Self-Stabilizing Graph Linearization with Untrusted Advice
L10: 
L11: Authors:cite5†Vijeth Aradhya , cite6†Christian Scheideler L12: 
L13: View a PDF of the paper titled Towards Learning-Augmented Peer-to-Peer Networks: Self-Stabilizing Graph Linearization with Untrusted Advice, by Vijeth Aradhya and 1 other authors
L14: 
L15: cite7†View PDF cite8†HTML (experimental) L16: > Abstract:Distributed peer-to-peer systems are widely popular due to their decentralized nature, which ensures that no peer is critical for the functionality of the system. However, fully decentralized solutions are usually much harder to design, and tend to have a much higher overhead compared to centralized approaches, where the peers are connected to a powerful server. On the other hand, centralized approaches have a single point of failure.
L17: Thus, is there some way to combine their advantages without inheriting their disadvantages? To that end, we consider a supervised peer-to-peer approach where the peers can ask a potentially unreliable supervisor for advice. This is in line with the increasingly popular algorithmic paradigm called algorithms with predictions or learning-augmented algorithms, but we are the first to consider it in the context of peer-to-peer networks.
L18: > Specifically, we design self-stabilizing algorithms for the fundamental problem of distributed graph linearization, where peers are supposed to recover the "sorted line" network from any initial network after a transient fault. With the help of the supervisor, peers can recover the sorted line network in $O(\log n)$ time, if the advice is correct; otherwise, the algorithm retains its original recovery time (i.e., without any supervisor).
L19: A crucial challenge that we overcome is to correctly compose multiple self-stabilizing algorithms, that is, one that processes and exploits the advice, and another that does not rely on the advice at all. Our key technical contributions combine ideas from the fields of overlay networks and proof-labeling schemes. Finally, we give a matching lower bound of $\Omega(\log n)$ for the recovery time of any algorithm if the advice can be corrupted, where $n$ is the network size.
